::: {.kw-overview}
Two strands dominate this issue, and they pull in opposite directions. The first is donor utilisation, where a national matched analysis of nearly 141,000 American transplants finds that putting both kidneys from a hard-to-place donor into one recipient outperforms single implantation once recipient age and kidney donor profile index are balanced, while a Brazilian cohort of just over 3,000 shows that the apparent penalty attached to deceased donors with diabetes evaporates after matching on donor age, hypertension and cause of death — two papers arguing, from different directions, that the organ most units hesitate over is usually being judged on the company it keeps rather than on itself. A third takes the same lens to living donation and finds a real if modest cost: in 88,490 living donor transplants, any donor smoking history carried a 13% higher hazard of graft loss, rising to 29% beyond twenty pack-years. The second strand is access, where the French registry shows that an acceptable mismatch programme gives highly sensitised candidates transplant rates approaching those of unsensitised patients without any graft survival penalty, and a JAMA cohort of 630,848 Medicare beneficiaries shows how much of the inequity in American transplantation is decided before a candidate ever reaches the list. The remaining three are immunological: a narrative review arguing that donor-specific antibody-negative, C4d-negative microvascular inflammation is an endothelial injury phenotype rather than one disease, a national immunosuppression guideline written on the premise that no comprehensive international consensus has appeared since KDIGO's in 2009, and a small but striking series in which six stable recipients were taken off immunosuppression years after their transplant through delayed stem cell chimerism.
:::

### 1. [Dual versus Single Kidney Transplantation in Contemporary U.S. Practice: A National Matched Cohort Study](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.70687)
[Koura AA, Judd A, Silpe S, Guerra JF, Ladie D, Brayman K, Pelletier SJ, Al-Adwan Y. *Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42767669.]{.kw-ref}

Dual implantation is the obvious answer to a kidney with too few nephrons for one recipient, and it is almost never done — in this national series it accounted for 1,236 of 140,707 adult deceased donor transplants performed between March 2015 and December 2024, or 0.9%. The crude comparison looks discouraging and explains much of the reluctance: dual recipients had more delayed graft function (38.9% versus 31.6%) and lower graft survival at one, three and five years (92.8%, 82.5% and 71.3% against 93.2%, 84.7% and 74.5%). That comparison is not a fair one, because the two groups are not remotely alike — dual donors averaged 54.8 years against 40.5, were hypertensive in 59.8% of cases against 30.0%, had a kidney donor profile index of 85 or above in 37.5% against 5.6%, and came with cold ischaemic times of 23.2 hours against 18.8. After 2:1 propensity matching on recipient age, kidney donor profile index, primary renal diagnosis and donor interstitial fibrosis, leaving 1,105 dual and 2,210 single recipients with mean recipient age 63.7 against 63.9 and kidney donor profile index 75.5 against 75.8, the direction reverses: graft survival at one, three and five years was 92.2%, 81.8% and 69.8% for dual against 87.7%, 75.5% and 59.9% for single, patient survival 95.1%, 86.3% and 75.7% against 92.6%, 82.2% and 66.8%, and delayed graft function was no different at 40.5% against 40.7%. Estimated glomerular filtration rate at one year was 58.9 mL/min/1.73 m² in dual recipients against 46.2 in single, and the fully adjusted matched hazard of graft failure was 0.731 (95% confidence interval 0.630 to 0.849). Two cautions matter more than the headline. Median follow-up was only 2.2 years in the dual group and 2.1 in the single group, so the five-year Kaplan-Meier estimates rest on a thin tail; and cold ischaemic time remained imbalanced after matching (23.45 against 20.78 hours, standardised mean difference 0.319), which if anything biases against dual transplantation but was not matched away. The authors are also explicit that allocation to dual implantation is a centre-level decision shaped by surgeon judgement and acceptance thresholds that the registry does not record, and that every dual transplant costs a second recipient their chance. For a UK unit the question this sharpens is not whether dual transplantation works but when it is being considered at all: if an older candidate's realistic alternative to a high-kidney-donor-risk-index pair is continued dialysis rather than a better single offer, these data suggest the arithmetic deserves revisiting earlier in the offering process than it usually is.

### 2. [Five-Year Outcomes and Clinicopathological Correlations of Kidney Transplants From Deceased Donors With Diabetes](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.70698)
[Colella-Santos M, Pepato PH, Proença HMS, Moura LAR, Medina-Pestana J, Foresto RD, Requião-Moura L. *Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42804549.]{.kw-ref}

Donor diabetes is treated almost everywhere as a quality marker rather than a diagnosis, and this single-centre Brazilian cohort tests whether the label survives adjustment for everything that travels with it. Among 3,058 adult recipients of brain-death donor kidneys transplanted at a high-volume São Paulo centre between 2013 and 2017, 244 (8.0%) came from donors with diabetes, and those donors were older (median 56 against 48 years), hypertensive in 79.9% of cases against 37.3%, dead from stroke in 75.4% against 59.2%, and carried a median kidney donor profile index of 92.5% against 67.0%. Unadjusted, their recipients did worse by every measure: estimated glomerular filtration rate was 37.8 mL/min/1.73 m² at year one and 30.3 at year five, against 46.3 and 39.8 in recipients of non-diabetic donor kidneys, an overall adjusted mean difference of −9.26 (95% confidence interval −11.90 to −6.63), and five-year death-censored graft survival was 76.1% against 85.0%. After 1:2 propensity matching on donor age, donor hypertension, cause of brain death and HLA-DR compatibility, both differences disappeared — mean estimated glomerular filtration rate differed by −2.30 (−5.37 to 0.78) and five-year death-censored graft survival was 76.1% against 78.9% — and the rate of functional decline between years one and five was the same in both arms (−7.52 against −6.48 mL/min/1.73 m²). The pattern the authors draw out is worth holding onto: these kidneys start with less functional reserve but do not deteriorate faster, so a lower first-year estimated glomerular filtration rate should not be read as evidence of progressive donor-derived diabetic injury. Pre-implantation histology, available for 164 of the 238 biopsied diabetic donor kidneys, showed no glomerular basement membrane change at all, mesangial expansion in 1.8%, absent interstitial fibrosis or tubular atrophy in around 70%, but fibrous intimal thickening in 63.4% and arteriolar hyalinosis in 59.1% — and no Banff chronicity parameter independently predicted either an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 30 mL/min/1.73 m² or death-censored graft loss at five years, echoing last week's systematic review of time-zero biopsy from the opposite direction. The limitations are real: kidney donor profile index and kidney donor risk index remained higher in the diabetic group even after matching, donor diabetes duration and HbA1c were unavailable, only 39 recipients fell into the diabetic-donor-into-diabetic-recipient cell that other registries have flagged as high risk, and the biopsy cohort by construction excludes the kidneys that histology persuaded the team to decline. Read alongside the dual transplantation paper above, the practical message for a UK surgeon is the same in both: donor diabetes is a prompt to assemble the whole risk profile, not a sufficient reason to turn the offer down.

### 3. [Impact of Cigarette Smoking among Living Donors on Kidney Transplant Graft Survival](https://doi.org/10.34067/KID.0000001402)
[McBee MK, Tancredi DJ, Butani L. *Kidney360*, 2026. PMID: 42821333.]{.kw-ref}

Every living donor assessment asks about smoking, and until now the honest answer to a donor who asks what difference it makes to the recipient has been that the literature disagrees with itself. This retrospective cohort used the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network database to follow 88,490 living donor kidney-only transplants performed between June 2004 and June 2022, taking donor smoking history as the exposure in several forms — ever against never, former against active, pack-years, and years of abstinence — with all-cause graft loss as the primary outcome in multivariable Cox models and delayed graft function and first-year acute rejection as secondary outcomes in logistic models. Any donor smoking history was associated with a higher hazard of graft loss (hazard ratio 1.13, 95% confidence interval 1.09 to 1.16) and higher odds of acute rejection in the first year (odds ratio 1.18, 1.11 to 1.25). The gradient behaved as the hypothesis predicted: against never-smokers, active smoking carried a hazard ratio of 1.19 (1.13 to 1.25) and former smoking 1.10 (1.07 to 1.14), with the difference between active and former itself significant, and donors with more than twenty pack-years produced the worst results across all three outcomes — graft loss 1.29 (1.21 to 1.37), delayed graft function 1.24 (1.03 to 1.49) and acute rejection 1.31 (1.16 to 1.50). The effect sizes are modest in relative terms and the authors say so, describing the increase as modest rather than prohibitive; this is not an argument for declining smokers as donors. What it does provide is a dose-response structure for a conversation that has until now been conducted on principle alone. The usual registry caveats apply with force here: smoking history is self-reported at donation, abstinence duration still more so, and residual confounding by recipient smoking and shared household or socioeconomic factors cannot be excluded in a database that was not designed to capture them. For a UK living donor programme the usable conclusions are that cessation before donation is worth pressing for because former smokers did measurably better than active ones, that pack-year burden rather than smoking status is the variable to record, and that a donor with a heavy history should prompt a frank conversation with the recipient rather than a refusal.

### 4. [Improved access to kidney transplantation with favorable graft survival in highly sensitized candidates under the French acceptable mismatch program](https://doi.org/10.3389/ti.2026.16762)
[Antoine C, Savoye E, Audry B, Legeai C, Pastural M, Cesbron A, Dubois V, Taupin JL. *Transpl Int*, 2026. PMID: 42774134.]{.kw-ref}

The standing objection to prioritising highly sensitised candidates is that the organs they eventually receive are immunologically compromised, so equity is bought at the cost of utility — and this analysis of the French national registry is the most complete answer to that objection yet published. France defines a highly sensitised candidate as one with a peak calculated reaction frequency of 85% or more and a current value above 70%, and since 2005 has run an acceptable mismatch programme, enhanced in 2015, that permits up to four HLA-A, -B, -DR and -DQβ mismatches provided every one of them is an antigen the candidate has no antibody against, with a negative virtual crossmatch mandatory before the organ moves. Access, measured as cumulative incidence of transplantation at 36 months among candidates listed between 2016 and 2023, was 49% (95% confidence interval 49 to 50) for unsensitised candidates, 52% (50 to 55) for first-transplant candidates with a peak calculated reaction frequency of 85–97% and 43% (40 to 45) for their retransplant equivalents, falling to 24% (21 to 28) and 14% (12 to 16) in the 98–100% band — with a visible inflection in the curve at around 18 months, the point at which programme eligibility begins. Across 2,985 single-organ brain-death donor transplants in highly sensitised adults between 2016 and 2022, followed for a mean of 45.5 months, death-censored graft survival under the programme was statistically indistinguishable from that of unsensitised recipients (log-rank p = 0.1185), while recipients allocated outside it did worse (p = 0.0125), and after Cox adjustment the hazard of graft failure for non-programme allocation was 1.19 (1.04 to 1.36), or 1.31 (1.08 to 1.59) death-censored, holding at 1.28 (1.05 to 1.55) when a centre effect was added. The gradient extended to historical antibody: five-year death-censored graft survival was 85.6% (83.4 to 87.5) under the programme, 81.7% (79.0 to 84.0) outside it without a previously delisted donor-specific antibody, and 75.4% (61.2 to 85.0) where such an antibody had been delisted during the wait. Two structural findings deserve attention beyond the allocation question: the proportion of highly sensitised patients on the active list fell from 28% to 17% between 2016 and 2025, which the authors attribute to better class-II matching in young recipients and more disciplined antibody interpretation rather than to any change in how the calculated reaction frequency is derived; and women made up 57% of highly sensitised candidates against 34% of unsensitised ones, so a programme of this design is also a sex-equity intervention. The authors are candid that the registry's rejection and graft-loss-cause fields are neither mandatory nor audited, so no mechanistic claim can be made, and that the comparison remains observational. For UK readers the relevance is direct and uncomfortable: the paper demonstrates that an acceptable-mismatch route can be added to a national scheme without the graft survival penalty that has always been the reason not to, and the patients it helps most — first-transplant candidates with common HLA phenotypes and broad class-I sensitisation, most of them women sensitised by pregnancy — are a group every UK unit can name.

### 5. [Medicare Advantage Enrollment and Access to Kidney Transplant After the 21st Century Cures Act](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2026.14391)
[Shah AD, Dana BA, Brazier JF, Tyler DA, Kim D, Nguyen KH, Meyers DJ, Drewry K, Lee Y, Wilk AS, Mehrotra R, Gadbois EA, Rivera-Hernandez M, Patzer RE, Trivedi AN. *JAMA*, 2026. PMID: 42766312.]{.kw-ref}

The 21st Century Cures Act let American patients with end-stage kidney disease enrol in Medicare Advantage, the managed-care alternative to traditional Medicare, and this retrospective cohort asks what that did to their chance of being transplanted. The study followed 630,848 Medicare beneficiaries aged 18 to 74 with end-stage kidney disease who had not received a transplant in the previous three years, from 1 January 2021 to 31 December 2023 — mean age 57.9 years (standard deviation 11.0), 40.9% female, 35.2% Black, 19.4% Hispanic — across 14.8 million person-months, adjusting for demographics, dual Medicare-Medicaid eligibility, duration of end-stage kidney disease, socioeconomic status and hospital referral region. Transplant rates were 2.51 per 1,000 person-months under Medicare Advantage against 4.60 under traditional Medicare, an adjusted rate ratio of 0.71 (95% confidence interval 0.69 to 0.72) that was essentially identical in each of the three years and widest in absolute terms among the youngest beneficiaries. Incident waitlisting showed the same pattern (3.05 against 4.64 per 1,000 person-months; adjusted rate ratio 0.77, 0.75 to 0.78). The analysis that locates the problem is the third one: among beneficiaries already waitlisted, the gap narrowed sharply to an adjusted rate ratio of 0.91 (0.90 to 0.92), which says that most of the shortfall is generated upstream of the transplant list rather than at the point of allocation. This is an observational comparison of people who chose different insurance products, so selection on health status and on the characteristics that drive plan choice cannot be excluded, and the authors make no causal claim — they argue for policy oversight rather than attributing the gap to any specific plan behaviour. The UK has no analogue to Medicare Advantage, but it does have the same structural problem in a different costume: this paper is a large, clean demonstration that where a health system places its gatekeeping — at referral and assessment rather than at allocation — determines where its inequity accumulates, and that a national allocation scheme can be scrupulously fair and still sit downstream of a funnel that is not.

### 6. [DSA-negative, C4d-negative microvascular inflammation after kidney transplantation as an endothelial injury syndrome: A narrative review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trre.2026.101056)
[El Hennawy HM, Safar O, Aboalsamh G, Banemah T, Almarzouk S, Neyas A, El Hennawy M, Khedr A, Sharab AM, Jaber T, Abudawood R, Balah R, Tawahri I. *Transplant Rev (Orlando)*, 2026. PMID: 42822228.]{.kw-ref}

Glomerulitis and peritubular capillaritis in a biopsy with no donor-specific antibody and no C4d is one of the more uncomfortable results in transplant nephrology: the Banff 2022 classification recognises the category, but it offers no mechanism, no prognosis and no treatment. This narrative review, built on a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library from January 2000 to June 2026 with qualitative synthesis and no pooling, assembles what is known and argues that the category is not one disease. The prognostic case is strong: in the largest multicentre series it draws on, more than 16,000 biopsies from around 6,900 recipients across more than thirty centres, the graft-loss hazard associated with donor-specific antibody-negative microvascular inflammation was 2.1 (95% confidence interval 1.5 to 3.1) against 2.7 (2.2 to 3.3) for antibody-mediated rejection itself, with graft-failure rates across the literature ranging from 18% to 48%. Several threads point to distinct mechanisms converging on the same histology: molecularly defined antibody-negative antibody-mediated rejection presented earlier than its antibody-positive counterpart (2.4 against 3.9 years), early microvascular inflammation was donor-specific-antibody-associated in only 27% of cases against 79% of late biopsies, missing-self allorecognition of at least one type was associated with microvascular inflammation (odds ratio 1.40, 1.08 to 1.80), and pre-transplant anti-angiotensin II type 1 receptor antibodies predicted rejection with a hazard ratio of 2.09. A single-centre Japanese cohort also linked lower tacrolimus (odds ratio 0.169) and everolimus exposure (0.386) to microvascular inflammation, which the authors are careful to label hypothesis-generating pending multicentre replication — and the missing-self association with graft loss itself did not reach significance (hazard ratio 1.97, 0.89 to 4.37). The review's contribution is a framework rather than a finding: an Endothelial Injury Continuum Model under which these pathways are organised by their shared downstream phenotype, with "endothelial injury syndrome" proposed as a descriptor explicitly not intended to displace any Banff category, and prospective multicentre validation named as the prerequisite before any of it guides treatment. For a UK transplant surgeon the immediate value is in how such a biopsy is discussed at the multidisciplinary meeting: the graft-loss hazard is close enough to that of frank antibody-mediated rejection that a negative antibody screen is no reason for reassurance, while the heterogeneity the review documents is reason enough not to reach reflexively for antibody-directed therapy.

### 7. [Thai Transplant Care Practice Guideline on Immunosuppressive Therapy for Adult Kidney Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1111/nep.70268)
[Udomkarnjananun S, Sutharattanapong N, Larpparisuth N, Phonphok K, Ngamvichchukorn T, Skulratanasak P, Inkong P, Wongpraphairot S, Traitanon O, Homkrailas P, Noppakun K, Townamchai N. *Nephrology (Carlton)*, 2026. PMID: 42813300.]{.kw-ref}

The most striking claim in this document is in its rationale rather than its recommendations: the authors point out that there has been no updated comprehensive international consensus on immunosuppression in kidney transplantation since the KDIGO guideline of 2009, more than seventeen years ago, and set out to fill that gap. The Thai Transplantation Society's guideline covers the full span of immunosuppressive practice — induction, maintenance, therapeutic drug monitoring and the treatment of rejection — and is explicitly written both as a national standard and as a template for low- and middle-income countries in the Asia-Pacific and Southeast Asian region, where the authors note that genetic profiles and resource constraints both argue against importing North American or European protocols unmodified. Two elements have no counterpart in existing guidance. The first is a set of cost-reduction protocols built around generic agents and the deliberate co-administration of cytochrome P450 3A4 and 3A5 inhibitors to reduce the calcineurin inhibitor dose required to hit target — a practice that happens informally in many programmes but has not previously been written down as policy. The second is structured guidance for clinical situations most guidelines leave to local improvisation: immunosuppression during periods of fasting, in pregnancy, and in the presence of malignancy. The abstract is a scope statement rather than a summary of recommendations, so the strength of evidence behind individual statements, and whether the pharmacokinetic boosting strategy is supported by trial data or by pharmacology alone, cannot be judged without the full document — and a guideline calibrated to Thai CYP3A5 expressor frequencies will not transfer unexamined to a UK population. Even so, the fasting and pregnancy chapters address questions that come up in every UK transplant clinic with a substantial Muslim or female-of-childbearing-age population and have no authoritative national answer, which makes this worth reading well outside the region it was written for.

### 8. [Delayed immune tolerance intentionally achieved years after two-haplotype matched kidney transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.09.021)
[Lum EL, Nassiri N, Oliai C, Raldow AC, Reed EF, Veale J. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42763042.]{.kw-ref}

Tolerance protocols have until now been something you either did at the time of transplantation or did not do at all: combined kidney and donor stem cell transplantation has achieved immunosuppression withdrawal in transplant-naïve recipients, but only when the stem cell infusion followed the kidney within about two weeks. This series asks whether the window is really that narrow, taking six healthy, stable, HLA-matched kidney transplant recipients who were already years past their operation and putting them through nonmyeloablative conditioning and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation from their original donor. All six engrafted, all achieved durable mixed donor chimerism, all were withdrawn from immunosuppression, and none developed graft-versus-host disease — which, given that graft-versus-host disease is the complication that has historically made this trade unattractive, is the most important of those statements. At publication five remained immunosuppression-free, one of them for over three years, and allograft function improved in every patient once immunosuppression was stopped. The sixth rejected after fifteen months off treatment and required maintenance immunosuppression to be restarted, which is the honest counterweight: a one-in-six failure rate in a highly selected group, and no indication yet of how long the five will hold. The design limits are severe and the authors state them plainly — six patients, HLA-matched siblings only, and no control group — so this is a proof of concept rather than a protocol, and the two-haplotype-matched population it applies to is small in any UK programme. What makes it worth a consultant's attention is the conceptual point rather than the numbers: if tolerance can be induced years after the fact, then the decision not to pursue it at the time of transplantation is no longer irreversible, and the conversation with a young matched-sibling recipient facing fifty years of calcineurin inhibitor exposure changes shape.
